mcqs.question: Why should a team default to a single region instead of starting multi-region?
options: Multi-region adds ongoing replication, consistency, and operational cost that only pays off against a specific force
Cloud providers technically don't allow new accounts to deploy to more than one region
A single region always has lower per-request latency than any multi-region setup, everywhere
Multi-region is only a marketing term and has no real architectural difference from single-region
mcqs.explanation: Multi-region is a real architecture with a real, ongoing cost — replication, conflict handling, doubled infrastructure — so it should be adopted only when a specific force justifies it, not by default. There's no such provider restriction, single-region can't beat multi-region for distant users, and multi-region is architecturally distinct, not just marketing.

mcqs.question: Users in Singapore see much higher latency than users in the US on a service running only in us-east-1. What's the correct first move?
options: Add more app servers in us-east-1 to reduce request queueing
Deploy a region physically closer to Singapore, since the gap is network distance, not compute capacity
Upgrade the database instance size in us-east-1
Enable more aggressive response compression to cut payload size
mcqs.explanation: Distance-driven latency is set by the speed of light in fiber and can't be fixed by more compute or a bigger database in the existing region — those help capacity problems, not geography problems. Compression can shave some bytes but doesn't touch the physical round-trip floor. A region near the affected users is the actual fix.

mcqs.question: A team says "we have a backup region" but failover takes 40 minutes of manual scripted cutover. What does this architecture actually provide?
options: True multi-region, since a second region exists and can take over
Active-active multi-region, since both regions contain the same infrastructure
Single-region with a backup region — not true multi-region, since only one region serves live traffic and failover is slow
No meaningful availability benefit over having no second region at all
mcqs.explanation: True multi-region means multiple regions actively serving traffic with fast, near-automatic failover. A 40-minute manual cutover with only one region live at a time is the single-region-plus-backup pattern — it does help availability versus having nothing, but it isn't the same guarantee as true multi-region.

mcqs.question: A service is CPU-saturated in its single region under current load, and the team proposes adding a second active region to handle the overflow. What's the flaw in this plan?
options: There is no flaw — spreading load across two regions is the standard fix for CPU saturation
The plan under-provisions the database, which multi-region doesn't address at all
Multi-region is only useful for data residency, never for availability or latency
Capacity saturation is a horizontal-scaling problem within the region; going multi-region adds replication and routing complexity without fixing the underlying under-provisioning
mcqs.explanation: Raw capacity problems are solved by scaling out inside the existing region — more nodes, shards, or replicas — not by adding geography. A second region on top of an under-scaled system just yields two under-scaled regions plus new cross-region complexity. Multi-region does help availability and latency too, just not capacity.
